explain.text:
The test rows are the last `n_test`, so cut at `len(rows) - n_test`. Writing `rows[:-n_test]` fails when `n_test` is 0, because `-0` is 0.

```python
cut = len(rows) - n_test
return (rows[:cut], rows[cut:])
```

items.title: Spot the leak
The 100% app
items.prompt:
A friend's app “predicts the Premier League with 100% accuracy”. They built it by trying thousands of rules on last season's 380 matches and keeping the one that got every result right. They want you to put £200 on its picks this season.

(a) What does the 100% tell you, and what does it not? (b) What would you ask them? (c) Describe a fair test, step by step. (d) What score on a fair test would you need before you risked money, and why can you not answer that from last season alone?
items.model:
**(a)** The 100% is a training score. The rule was chosen on the same 380 matches it is scored on, from thousands of tries. Like the memoriser, a rule picked that way can fit last season perfectly and still know nothing about new matches. It tells us the rule fits its own examples; it says nothing about this season.

**(b)** I would ask: which matches chose the rule, and were any matches kept back? How many rules were tried? What is its score on matches it never saw? Do its features use anything known only after kick-off, such as the half-time score? That would be a leak.

**(c)** A fair test:

1. Before choosing anything, put some matches aside, for example the last 80 of last season.
2. Choose the rule using the other 300 only.
3. Score it once on the 80. Do not change the rule after seeing that score.
4. Better still, score it on this season's first matches, written down before kick-off.

**(d)** The score must beat simple guesses, such as always picking the home team, on matches it never saw. Even then, 80 matches is a small test: a lucky run is possible. Last season alone cannot answer this, because every one of its matches helped choose the rule. Only kept-back or future matches can.

rubric.text: Says the 100% is a training score: the rule was chosen and scored on the same matches
Links this to the memoriser or to trying many rules: a perfect fit proves little about new matches
Asks a fair question: which matches were kept back, how many rules were tried, or whether any feature is a leak
Describes a fair test: keep matches back before choosing, choose on the rest, score once
Says a fair score must beat a simple guess on unseen matches, and that last season cannot supply it
